text: What if I already typed my password?
reply: Acting fast helps. Change that password and your account PIN right away in the official app or website, and anywhere you reused it. Call your carrier on the number from its official website or your bill. Report it and ask it to lock number transfers for SIM swap protection. Turn on 2-step verification, sign out other devices, and check for new devices or call forwarding. Watch your bank and card statements. Report the scam at ReportFraud.ftc.gov. Use IdentityTheft.gov if ID numbers were taken. Do not tap links or share codes.

text: Teach me why LEDs need resistors.
reply: The LED only drops about 2 volts, so without a resistor nothing limits the current and the LED would burn out. With 330 ohms, the resistor takes the remaining 7 volts and sets the current to about 21 milliamps, making the LED bright. This is a simplified model where the LED is treated as a fixed 2 volt drop.

facts.text: The series resistor takes the rest of the supply voltage and sets the current: I = (V_source − V_LED) / R.
Because an LED's voltage barely changes once it conducts, nothing in the LED itself limits the current; a series resistor has to set it.
With the same battery and LED, a 1,000 Ω resistor lowers the current to 7.0 mA, so the LED is dimmer.

source.title: TinyDirector calculation modules (director/circuit/model.py, director/lesson/calculators.py): the simplified models this tutor computes with

facts.text: An LED conducts in one direction only, from the anode (+, the longer leg) to the cathode (−, the shorter leg by the flat edge).
An LED's brightness follows its current: more current gives more light, up to its rating.
A typical 5 mm indicator LED is rated for about 20 mA of continuous current.
